frameworks.name: TWATS Office Model
frameworks.definition: A weekly partitioning structure where Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday are dedicated to face-to-face office work, with Monday and Friday reserved for location-independent individual work.

frameworks.name: Maker Schedule vs Manager Schedule
frameworks.definition: Paul Graham's distinction between managers (who optimize for maximum meeting density) and makers (who require large uninterrupted time blocks to produce creative or technical work), making half-hour meeting interruptions disproportionately costly for makers.

claims.text: Bruce Daisley asserts that stress in modern organizations afflicts people lower in the hierarchy more than those at the top, inverting the common assumption that bosses bear more stress. The mechanism is that lower-ranking employees have less control over their time, meetings, and email load, which produces what looks behaviorally identical to depression.
claims.speaker: Bruce Daisley
claims.mechanism: Lack of control over job tasks and time triggers a submissive behavioral pattern that is physiologically indistinguishable from depression; control is the variable, not rank.
bounded_by: Does not apply to senior leaders who have discretion over their schedules

claims.text: Bruce Daisley reports that the average British worker spends 16 hours per week in meetings, and that knowledge workers at senior levels likely exceed that average. Despite this, attention in those meetings is low enough that workers feel compelled to disguise distraction (e.g., checking Instagram) to appear engaged.
claims.speaker: Bruce Daisley

numbers.axis: hours per week in meetings by worker type

claims.text: Bruce Daisley argues that organizational scale systematically destroys the autonomy and social connection that motivate workers, because the coordination overhead of large organizations — driven by the Dunbar number limit of roughly 150 stable social relationships — wipes out any efficiency gains from scale.
claims.speaker: Bruce Daisley
claims.mechanism: Human social bandwidth caps at approximately 150 stable connections (Dunbar number); organizations larger than that generate coordination overhead that exceeds the economic benefit of scale while simultaneously eliminating the sense of autonomy and belonging that motivates performance.

numbers.axis: stable social connections per person (Dunbar number)

bounded_by: Manufacturing or highly codified assembly-line work may benefit from scale without the same social coordination cost

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that the Silicon Valley assumption that removing constraints is automatically good is a dangerous mental model when applied to human behavior. Physical and temporal constraints historically provided two benefits: focus (by limiting what activity was possible in a given setting) and coordination (by synchronizing activity across groups).
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: Constraints create focus by eliminating competing stimuli; they create coordination by aligning timing across groups. Removing both simultaneously eliminates the positive externalities that constraints provided, without a designed replacement.
bounded_by: Physical constraints on manufacturing and logistics genuinely benefit from removal
Applies to cognitive and social work, not purely mechanical tasks

claims.text: Rory Sutherland asserts that the mere presence of a mobile phone or notification in a meeting room reduces concentration even if the person does not look at it, because awareness that other activity is occurring elsewhere is itself cognitively disruptive.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: The knowledge that another channel of activity exists competes for attentional resources; even without overt distraction, divided attention baseline is set lower than in a device-absent environment.

claims.text: Rory Sutherland asserts that time is not fungible for cognitive work: ten one-hour blocks of time do not produce the same output as one ten-hour block, because creative and technical work requires sustained, uninterrupted flow states that short blocks cannot achieve. This is articulated in Paul Graham's Maker Schedule vs Manager Schedule framework.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: not applicable to managerial coordination tasks
claims.mechanism: Deep cognitive work requires extended uninterrupted time to enter flow and sustain it; any interruption effectively resets the setup cost for re-entering that state, making fragmented scheduling disproportionately costly.
bounded_by: Does not apply to managers whose work consists of many short discrete decisions
Physical manufacturing output is largely time-fungible

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that instant email delivery is an assumption, not a technical requirement, and its default instantaneous nature causes significant harm to recipients — particularly when senior leaders send emails on weekends intending them to be read Monday, but workers read them immediately and lose their weekend.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: email used as primary async communication
claims.mechanism: Default instantaneous delivery creates social pressure for immediate response regardless of the sender's intent; the psychological effect is indistinguishable from an explicit directive to respond now.
bounded_by: Emergency or on-call operational contexts where immediate notification is genuinely required

claims.text: Rory Sutherland proposes that intelligent partitioning of the working week — where location-independent tasks are concentrated on one or two days (e.g., Monday and Friday) and in-person collaborative work on the remaining days — would generate additional freedom and productivity benefits without reducing total output.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: where less than 80% of work is both place-dependent and time-dependent
claims.mechanism: Batching same-type work into dedicated time blocks eliminates the cognitive switching cost paid each time a worker shifts between synchronous collaboration and independent deep work.

numbers.axis: percentage of work that is place-dependent and time-dependent

anchors.value: less than 80% of knowledge work is both place- and time-dependent

bounded_by: Does not benefit organizations if everyone does different activities on different days, eliminating the coordination gains

claims.text: Bruce Daisley reports that at Twitter's London office circa 2015, approximately 40% of staff turned over in one year, with a notable portion resigning with no job to go to — indicating that even aspirational employers can generate enough workplace dysfunction to override the prestige of the employment brand.
claims.speaker: Bruce Daisley
claims.mechanism: Weekend emails and always-on norms created a perception of inescapability from work, analogous to behaviorally targeted ads following a user across the internet; the psychological exhaustion drove workers to leave even without alternative employment.

anchors.region: resignations with no job to go to

claims.text: Bruce Daisley asserts that when teams work face-to-face, they communicate approximately 40 times per week on a given project, versus approximately 8 times per week when working remotely — a 5:1 difference that represents lost coordination and refinement of shared work.
claims.speaker: Bruce Daisley
conditions: comparing co-located vs. remote working arrangements
claims.mechanism: Physical co-location enables spontaneous low-friction communication (corridor conversations, desk visits) that remote tools require deliberate scheduling to replicate; the scheduling friction reduces total communication volume by ~80%.

numbers.axis: informal communications per week between project team members

bounded_by: Applies to collaborative iterative work; may not apply to independent execution tasks where communication is not the primary coordination mechanism

claims.text: Rory Sutherland argues that batch processing email — checking it at four defined intervals per day rather than continuously — is the single greatest individual productivity improvement available, analogous to the Victorian postal system that delivered mail four times daily and was experienced as adequate.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
conditions: email as primary async communication channel
claims.mechanism: Continuous notification checking fragments attention into micro-interruptions that cumulatively degrade the quality and depth of non-email work; fixed-interval batch processing restores large uninterrupted blocks.
bounded_by: Does not apply to roles requiring real-time operational response (e.g., on-call engineering, customer support with SLA commitments)

claims.text: Bruce Daisley argues that 40 hours per week is sufficient for high-quality knowledge work output, and that people who work significantly more hours are not producing proportionally more value — they are confusing the feeling of difficulty or busyness with actual productivity.
claims.speaker: Bruce Daisley
claims.mechanism: Human cognitive resources are finite and zero-sum (ego depletion): after a threshold of sustained output, incremental hours produce diminishing or negative returns because the brain's decision-making and creative faculties are depleted. Workers mistake subjective difficulty for productivity because they use hardship as a proxy.

numbers.axis: weekly work hours vs. productive output quality

anchors.region: Bruce Daisley's modeled norm at Twitter

bounded_by: May not apply to physical labor or output-based manufacturing where hours directly correlate with units produced

claims.text: Rory Sutherland asserts that typing speed is dramatically slower than speech and that this difference is systematically underestimated, meaning that email resolves multi-party issues far more slowly than a 10-minute phone or video call — yet email feels productive because the user is typing at maximum typing speed.
claims.speaker: Rory Sutherland
claims.mechanism: Typing provides a false speed signal: users experience themselves as going fast (relative to other typing occasions) rather than slow (relative to speech). This misattribution causes workers and organizations to systematically prefer a slower modality because it feels effortful and therefore productive.

claims.text: Bruce Daisley argues that organizations driven by cost-reduction motives (hot-desking, work-from-home) trigger a gradual disconnection between individuals that accelerates over time, and that this disconnection is a predictable operational cost that is not accounted for in the cost-savings calculus.
claims.speaker: Bruce Daisley
conditions: organizations transitioning to remote or hot-desk models
claims.mechanism: Reduced physical proximity eliminates the spontaneous informal communications that refine shared work and maintain relational trust; the deficit compounds because each lost interaction reduces the baseline for the next, making the gap grow non-linearly.

claims.text: Bruce Daisley asserts that knowledge workers are poor at distinguishing between what feels difficult and what is productive, and that this confusion drives overwork. Manufacturing workers do not overwork to the same degree because their output is tangible and self-evidently countable, whereas knowledge work lacks clear completion signals.
claims.speaker: Bruce Daisley
claims.mechanism: Absence of visible output in knowledge work removes natural stopping signals; workers default to effort heuristics (am I working hard?) rather than output heuristics (have I produced the thing?), causing overwork that does not translate to proportional output.

examples.text: Bruce Daisley describes Nucor Steel, an American steel manufacturer started as a nuclear power company, which operates profitably by decentralizing all functions — marketing, recruitment, distribution — to individual mini-mills rather than running them centrally. The head office employs only 30 people for a large US manufacturer. Nucor found that the efficiency gains from centralized scale were an illusion; individual mini-mills, given autonomy over their own operations, outperformed the centralized model because workers felt control and ownership over their work.

Bruce Daisley describes Building 20 at MIT — a temporary wooden structure notorious for mice infestations and leaks — which over approximately 12 years produced nine Nobel Prize-winning physicists. Architect Bjarke Ingels cited it as inspiration for designing productive workplaces. The explanation Bruce offers is not aesthetic quality but self-organization: the building was informal enough that researchers arrived on weekends to install their own walls and create personalized spaces, enabling the small-team self-organization that drives creative productivity.

Rory Sutherland describes seeing miniaturized gas tankers in Mountain View, California — an Uber for gasoline service that refuels parked cars while engineers code. He uses this as a negative example of the Silicon Valley constraint-removal ideology: the service eliminates the petrol station stop but also removes the secondary value of that constraint (incidental purchases, a mental break, physical movement). He argues the designers see only the friction and not the positive externalities of the constraint.

Rory Sutherland describes David Ogilvy's practice of never writing advertising copy in the office — all his ads, body copy, and books were written at home. Ogilvy understood intuitively that his office time was for talking to people and managing them in series, while home time was for single-task deep focus. Rory uses this as evidence that the maker-manager distinction is not new, but previously emerged automatically from physical environment and now must be deliberately recreated.

Bruce Daisley describes a Twitter manager who liked fell-walking and would fire off a batch of emails early Saturday morning before heading out for the weekend, intending them to be read Monday. Two years later, his subordinates revealed that this practice ruined their entire weekends, because they felt obligated to read and respond. The sender's intent (deferred communication) was invisible; the receiver's experience (weekend work intrusion) was real. This illustrates the harm of default-instantaneous email delivery independent of the sender's intent.

Bruce Daisley describes a friend who is an architect and began sending clients a contract stating he only answers emails between 11am and 12pm each day. His first client under this contract was Paul Smith (the fashion designer), and after two days of silence the architect feared he had lost the client. Paul Smith's response was that it was the best contract he had ever received. Bruce uses this as evidence that high-status clients respect boundary-setting even when lower-status workers feel they cannot risk it.

practices.text: Switch notifications off on your phone as a default practice for sustained focus; audience show of hands at the event confirmed this was already adopted by a meaningful minority and those who did it found it significantly reduced distraction.

When in the office, restrict screen time to two hours per day and maximize face-to-face interactions; reserve home and remote time for screen-based individual work. This creates the coordination and communication density that office presence affords without sacrificing the deep-work capacity of independent time.

Organizations should configure email systems so that emails sent on weekends are not delivered until Monday by default, rather than requiring senders to remember to schedule-send. The default of instantaneous delivery is a design choice that can be reversed.

As a leader, model a 40-hour work week openly and publicly make it clear that stepping away from the desk is not a signal of poor performance. People take behavioral cues from leaders; visible modeling of boundaries creates permission for others to adopt the same.
